turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Kenji Watanabe. Can I get your full name and date of birth, please?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Priya Raghnathan, May 14th, 2002.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thanks Priya, quite the rain out there today. Did you get soaked?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A little, my umbrella flipped inside out on the way from the bus. Oh no,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: well, let's dry you off with some good news, hopefully. Your student health clinic sent you about palpitations.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, for about three weeks I've been feeling this like fluttering in my chest, or like my heart skips and then does a big thump.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: How long does each episode last?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Just a few seconds. It happens a bunch of times a day, mostly at night when I'm lying in bed.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Does it ever feel like a fast, steady racing that starts and stops suddenly?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, not really racing, more like skipping.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Have you fainted or felt like you were going to faint?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, never.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any chest pain or shortness of breath when it happens?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nope, it's just weird and it makes me anxious.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That makes sense. Tell me about your caffeine. How much coffee or energy drinks are you having?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, okay. So I'm in my second year of the pharmacy program at Lakeshore University, and finals prep has been rough. Probably four big cold brews a day, and then two energy drinks at night to keep studying. That's a lot of caffeine,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: probably well over 1 ,000 milligrams a day. How much are you sleeping?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe five hours, sometimes less. Any alcohol,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: vaping or other drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: A glass of wine on weekends sometimes. I don't smoke or vape.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Medicines?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Just my birth control pill once a day and I take melatonin 3 milligrams on nights I can't fall asleep. No allergies.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any heart problems in the family or anyone who died suddenly when they were young?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No heart stuff that I know of. My mom has a thyroid problem Hashimoto's she takes a pill for it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay good to know. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 118 over 74 pulse 88 oxygen 99 percent. Your thyroid doesn't feel enlarged. No tremor in your hands. Heart has a regular rhythm. No murmurs or clicks. Lungs are clear.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: We also did an ECG at check -in. It's a normal ECG, sinus rhythm at 84, with normal intervals and no signs of an extra electrical pathway.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So my heart is okay.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Everything I'm seeing looks healthy. What you're describing sounds like extra beats, early beats from the top or bottom chambers which are very common and usually harmless. The big triggers are caffeine, energy drinks, and not enough sleep and you've got all three going on.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that's fair.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: So here's the plan. I'd like you to cut back the caffeine gradually over the next two weeks so you don't get withdrawal headaches. Aim for no more than one regular coffee a day and and no energy drinks at all, and try to get at least seven hours of sleep.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can try. Finals end the 12th of December, so it'll get easier after that.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Fair, I'm also ordering a thyroid test,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a TSH,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: plus a blood count and electrolytes, just to rule out anything simple. If the palpitations are still happening in six weeks after you've cut back, we'll put a two -week patch monitor on you to record your rhythm. Okay, what number do you have for me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I changed phones.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's still right.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good, if you ever faint, or have chest pain with the fluttering, or a racing heartbeat that won't stop, go to the emergency room. Otherwise, I'll see you back in six weeks.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you, that's a relief honestly.
